cards.explanation: The answer is that David asks God to deliver him from his enemies. He opens with “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God…” (Psalm 59:1). Saul, Israel's king, has sent men to watch his house, and David's first move is to talk to God. No speech, no scheme, just a prayer. I think that's a good order to do things in, friends.

The answer is True. David says it plainly: “Fierce men conspire against me for no transgression or sin of my own, O LORD.” (Psalm 59:3). He says the same thing again in the next verse, “For no fault of my own…” (Psalm 59:4). That's two verses in a row where he tells God he's done nothing to deserve this. I think when your house is being watched, you say it twice.

The answer is no mercy. David asks the LORD to “show no mercy to the wicked traitors.” (Psalm 59:5). That's a heavy line, and I think it comes from a man who is scared and hurting. And it's right there in the verse, plain as flour on an apron, friends.

The word is city. David says his enemies return in the evening, “…snarling like dogs and prowling around the city.” (Psalm 59:6). Dogs on the loose in the middle of town is a scary picture, and that's the picture David paints, friends. Verse 14 says it again.

The answer is that they think nobody can hear them. Their own words give them away: “For who can hear us?” (Psalm 59:7). They talk like nobody is listening. But one verse later, David says of the LORD, “But You, O LORD, laugh at them…” (Psalm 59:8). It's like trash-talking your boss in the break room while the boss stands right behind you.

The answer is False. The LORD isn't afraid of them. David says, “But You, O LORD, laugh at them; You scoff at all the nations.” (Psalm 59:8). The men were saying, “For who can hear us?” (Psalm 59:7), and now David says that God laughs at them. Nobody here scares Him, friends.

The answer is God. David says, “I will keep watch for You, O my strength…” (Psalm 59:9). Saul's men are watching his house, and David turns around and watches for God. He gives his reason in the same verse: “…because You, O God, are my fortress.” I'd say that's a fine pick for who to watch for, friends.

The answer is True. David says, “God will let me stare down my foes.” (Psalm 59:10). It comes right after “My God of loving devotion will come to meet me…” So David is counting on God to come to him, friends.

The answer is so his people won't forget. David gives his reason right in the verse: “Do not kill them, or my people will forget.” (Psalm 59:11). Then he asks God to “Scatter them by Your power…” instead. It's a strange prayer at first, friends, but the reason is right there in the verse.

The answer is their pride and lies. David asks, “…let them be trapped in their pride, in the curses and lies they utter.” (Psalm 59:12). Right before that, he mentions the sins of their mouths and the words of their lips. It lines up with the sharp words from verse 7. Pride and lies are the ones he names, friends.

The answer is to the ends of the earth. David wants it known “…to the ends of the earth that God rules over Jacob.” (Psalm 59:13). That's a big wish for a man whose house is being watched. His eyes are on much more than his own street, and I think that's worth noticing, friends.

The word is morning. David says, “But I will sing of Your strength and proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning.” (Psalm 59:16). The enemies return in the evening, and David says he will sing in the morning. He sets a song right next to all that snarling. I think that's something to keep in your pocket, friends.

The answer is False. David says, “For You are my fortress, my refuge in times of trouble.” (Psalm 59:16). He's saying God is his refuge when things are hard, not only when they're easy. And with Saul's men watching his house, things were hard, friends.
